chapter.name: The World of Metals and Non-metals

questions.q: Anil says, 'Gold and silver are the most malleable metals, but iron can also be hammered into shape. That is why an ironsmith can beat a heated iron block into an axe.' Do you agree? Support your answer from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. Gold and silver are the most malleable, but most metals are malleable to some degree. Iron flattens when beaten (Activity 4.1 iron nail), so the ironsmith can shape it into an axe.
s: Verdict: agrees
Most metals are malleable, gold and silver the most
Iron flattens under the hammer, as in the activity and the ironsmith's work

questions.q: A pea-sized lump of a dull material is hammered. It crumbles into small pieces. What should the student record?
questions.a: A dull lump that breaks into pieces is brittle and non-lustrous, as sulfur is. A malleable material would flatten; wood does not break.
o: Non-lustrous and brittle, like sulfur
Lustrous and malleable, like gold
Soft but malleable, like sodium
Neither malleable nor brittle, like wood

questions.q:
At a school science fair, Kavya's stall shows silver foil on a sweet, a thermometer containing mercury, and a piece of sodium that her teacher cuts with a knife. Two signs are proposed for the stall. Sign 1: 'All metals are hard solids.' Sign 2: 'Metals are generally lustrous, hard and malleable, but a few are exceptions.'
(a) Name the property that lets silver be made into thin foil.
(b) Which two exhibits are exceptions to 'hard solid', and how does each differ?
(c) Choose Sign 1 or Sign 2 for the stall and justify your choice with the exhibits.
questions.a: (a) Malleability. (b) Mercury is a liquid at room temperature; sodium is soft enough to cut with a knife. (c) Sign 2: the exhibits show exceptions, so 'All metals are hard solids' is false, whereas 'generally' is true.
s: Part (a): malleability
Part (b): mercury liquid and sodium soft
Part (c): chooses sign 2 and justifies

questions.q:
Gurpreet's grandfather, a village blacksmith in Punjab, heats an iron bar in a coal furnace and beats it into a sickle blade. At school Gurpreet hammers four samples. P is shiny, hard and flattens. Q is dull, soft and breaks into pieces. R is dull and neither flattens nor breaks. S is shiny, soft enough to be cut with a knife and kept in kerosene by the teacher.
(a) Which of the samples P, Q, R and S are metals?
(b) Name the property shown by P and the property shown by Q on hammering.
(c) Gurpreet says S cannot be a metal because it is soft. Is he right? Give one reason.
(d) The blacksmith needs one material for a blade and one for its handle from P, Q and R. Choose for each and justify.
questions.a: (a) P and S are metals; Q and R are not metals (Q breaks, R neither flattens nor breaks). (b) P is malleable; Q is brittle. (c) No. Some metals such as sodium and potassium are soft enough to cut with a knife. (d) Blade: P, a hard malleable metal like iron. Handle: R, wood-like material (blacksmiths use wood for handles); Q would break.
s: Part (a): identifies P and S as metals
Part (b): malleable and brittle
Part (c): soft metals exist, e.g. sodium
Part (d): blade P, handle R, with reasons

questions.q: The shine shown by a freshly cleaned copper vessel is called
questions.a: The shine shown by metals is called metallic lustre. Malleability, sonority and ductility are other properties.
o: lustre
malleability
sonority
ductility

questions.q: Define metallic lustre and name two lustrous materials and two non-lustrous materials from Activity 4.1.
questions.a: Lustre shown by metals is metallic lustre. Lustrous: copper, aluminium (or iron). Non-lustrous: coal, sulfur (or wood).
s: Definition of metallic lustre
Two lustrous and two non-lustrous examples

questions.q: Which metal is found in the liquid state at room temperature?
questions.a: Mercury is the metal that is liquid at room temperature (as in thermometers). Sodium and potassium are solid but soft.
o: Mercury
Sodium
Potassium
Silver

questions.q: Write a short everyday situation (two or three sentences) in which a metal's malleability is useful, and another in which a non-metal's brittleness is easy to observe.
questions.a: Example: aluminium is beaten into thin foil to wrap tiffin food. A lump of coal or sulfur hit with a hammer crumbles into pieces.
s: A situation using a malleable metal
A situation showing a brittle non-metal
Names the properties correctly

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Wood is neither malleable nor brittle.
Reason (R): Coal breaks into pieces when it is hammered.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but coal's behaviour says nothing about wood. Wood neither flattens nor breaks, so R does not explain A.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Meena hammers a block of a material on a hard surface. It neither becomes flat nor breaks into pieces. Which material was most likely used?
questions.a: Wood is neither malleable nor brittle. Coal and sulfur break into pieces; aluminium flattens.
o: A block of wood
A piece of coal
A lump of sulfur
A piece of aluminium

questions.q: The chapter says iron became important to Indian farming. Why were iron ploughs considered much superior to the ones used before?
questions.a: Iron is strong, so ploughs made of iron were much superior. The chapter notes this happened once iron came into everyday use, which took a long time.
s: Names strength of iron as the reason
Links it to ploughs / agricultural tools becoming superior

questions.q:
(a) Define malleability.
(b) Using your definition, say what happens when a lump of coal is hammered and name that behaviour.
questions.a: (a) The property by which a material can be beaten into thin sheets. (b) Coal does not flatten; it breaks into pieces and is called brittle.
s: Part (a): beaten into thin sheets
Part (b): coal breaks into pieces, so brittle

questions.q: Which statement about metals is FALSE?
questions.a: False: not all metals are hard solids - mercury is a liquid and sodium and potassium are cut with a knife. The others are true.
o: Every metal is a hard solid at room temperature.
Sodium and potassium are soft enough to be cut with a knife.
Gold and silver are the most malleable metals.
Shine shown by metals is called metallic lustre.

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I
1. Sodium
2. Mercury
3. Sulfur
4. Gold
Column II
a. Liquid at room temperature
b. Soft enough to cut with a knife
c. Most malleable metal (with silver)
d. Breaks into pieces when hammered
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-a, 3-d, 4-c. Sodium is cut with a knife, mercury is liquid, sulfur is brittle and gold is among the most malleable.

questions.q:
(a) Name the property that lets silver be made into thin foil for sweets.
(b) A sweet seller also wraps food in aluminium foil. What do the two foils tell you about the kind of materials that are made into sheets?
questions.a: (a) Malleability. (b) Both silver and aluminium are metals, and most metals are malleable, so metals are the materials made into sheets.
s: Part (a): malleability
Part (b): foils are metals, and most metals are malleable

questions.q: On being hammered, which pair of materials breaks into pieces instead of flattening?
questions.a: Coal and sulfur break into pieces (brittle). Copper, aluminium and iron flatten; wood neither flattens nor breaks.
o: Coal and sulfur
Copper and aluminium
Wood and coal
Iron and sulfur

questions.q: Sara hammers a block of wood and sees that it does not flatten. She says, 'So wood is brittle.' Do you agree? Explain with the chapter's two terms.
questions.a: No. A brittle material breaks into pieces. Wood neither flattens into a sheet (not malleable) nor breaks into pieces (not brittle).
s: Verdict: disagrees
Explains brittle means breaking into pieces
States wood is neither malleable nor brittle

questions.q: Differentiate between a malleable and a brittle material, giving one example of each.
questions.a: A malleable material flattens into thin sheets when beaten, e.g. aluminium or copper. A brittle material breaks into pieces when beaten, e.g. coal or sulfur.
s: Malleable: flattens into sheets, with example
Brittle: breaks into pieces, with example

questions.q: A teacher gives three metal pieces and three non-metal pieces, labelled P to U, and asks the class to separate them by lustre, hardness and the effect of hammering. Write the pattern you expect for metals (copper, aluminium, iron) and for non-metals (coal, sulfur, wood), and say whether one test alone can be trusted.
questions.a: Metals: lustrous, hard, flatten under the hammer. Coal and sulfur: non-lustrous, not as hard, break into pieces; wood non-lustrous, neither flattens nor breaks. One test alone is not reliable because some metals are soft (sodium, potassium) or liquid (mercury), so several properties must be used together.
s: Metals: lustrous, hard, flatten
Non-metals and wood: dull, softer, break or neither
Names an exception (sodium, potassium or mercury)
Concludes use several tests together

questions.q:
Read the statements about metals in early India.
Statement 1: The Harappans used copper and gold to make objects from utensils to jewellery.
Statement 2: Once iron came into common use, its strength made iron ploughs much better than the earlier ones.
Statement 3: Iron was widely used for daily objects in Harappan times, so evidence of it is easy to find.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 are true. 3 is false: hardly any evidence of iron is found at Harappan sites because it took a long time before iron was used day to day.
o: 1 and 2 only
2 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Asha says, 'The Harappans used copper and gold, but not iron. So they must have been less skilled with metals than people who used iron later.' Evaluate her statement using the chapter. Say what the chapter gives as the reason iron appears late and what difference iron made.
questions.a: The chapter says the Harappans used copper and gold for utensils and jewellery; iron came into day-to-day use only after a long time. So their not using iron is about when iron came into use, not a lack of skill with metals. Once it did, iron's strength made ploughs far superior. The statement is therefore an unfair conclusion.
s: Harappans did use copper and gold
Iron took a long time to come into day-to-day use
Iron's strength made ploughs superior later
Judges the statement unfair, as lack of iron does not show lack of skill

questions.q: Rahul says, 'If 1 g of gold gives a 2 km wire, then 3 g gives a 6 km wire, so a 9 km wire needs 4.5 g.' Is he right? Show your working.
questions.a: Yes. 3 x 2 = 6 km; and 9 / 2 = 4.5 g.
s: Uses 2 km per gram
Checks 3 g gives 6 km
Checks 9 km needs 4.5 g and agrees

questions.q:
(a) Define sonority.
(b) A vendor drops a coin on the counter to check it. Why does the ringing sound suggest it is metal?
questions.a: (a) The property of metals by which they give a ringing sound when struck. (b) Metals are sonorous; non-metals like coal and wood give a dull sound.
s: Part (a): ringing sound when struck
Part (b): metals ring, coal or wood sounds dull

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A school bell is made of metal.
Reason (R): Metals are sonorous and produce a ringing sound when struck.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both true; the ringing of the bell is due to sonority of the metal, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: One gram of gold can be drawn into a wire of length about
questions.a: The chapter says one gram of gold can be drawn into a wire 2 km long.
o: 2 kilometres
2 metres
20 kilometres
200 metres

questions.q: A seller says a thin string pulled out of a lump of coal will make a good sitar string. Show why this cannot work, using the properties of coal.
questions.a: Coal is not ductile, so it cannot be drawn into a wire. It is also brittle, breaking into pieces, and it gives a dull sound instead of the ringing sound that sonorous metals give.
s: Coal is not ductile
Coal is brittle
Dull sound against ringing

questions.q: Which statement about ductility and sonority is FALSE?
questions.a: False: wires of coal or sulfur are never seen; they are not ductile. The other statements match the chapter.
o: Coal and sulfur can be drawn into thin wires.
Veena and sitar strings make use of metal wires.
Ghungroos ring because metals are sonorous.
Steel ropes can carry heavy loads on cranes.

questions.q: Write a short situation in which both ductility and sonority of a metal are used.
questions.a: A sitar or veena has metal wires drawn from a ductile metal (ductility) and the struck string gives a ringing sound (sonority).
s: Names a suitable object
Explains ductility in it
Explains sonority in it

questions.q: Which material produces a dull sound when dropped on the floor?
questions.a: Coal and wood give dull sounds. Metals such as coins, spoons and bells ring (sonorous).
o: Coal
A metal coin
A metal spoon
A school bell

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Gold can be drawn into very long wires.
Reason (R): One gram of gold can be drawn into a wire only 2 metres long.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true (gold is very ductile). R is false: the chapter says one gram gives a wire 2 kilometres long.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: The property by which a material can be drawn into wires is called
questions.a: Drawing into wires is ductility. Malleability is beating into sheets; sonority is the ringing sound.
o: ductility
malleability
sonority
lustre

questions.q: Compare ductility and sonority. For each say what it means and give an object that shows it, and then say which of the two a suspension-bridge rope depends on.
questions.a: Ductility: drawn into wires (e.g. steel wires twisted into ropes). Sonority: ringing sound on striking (e.g. a bell). The bridge rope depends on ductility because steel wires form the rope that carries heavy loads.
s: Defines ductility with example
Defines sonority with example
Bridge rope depends on ductility
Reason: steel wires, heavy loads

questions.q: Differentiate between ductility and malleability with one example of each.
questions.a: Ductility is drawing into wires (copper wire); malleability is beating into thin sheets (aluminium foil).
s: Ductility: wires, with example
Malleability: sheets, with example

questions.q:
Read the statements about wires.
Statement 1: Copper and aluminium wires are used in electrical fittings because they are not ductile.
Statement 2: Steel is a mixture of iron (a metal) and carbon (a non-metal).
Statement 3: Ropes made of steel wires can support heavy loads in suspension bridges and cranes.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 are true. 1 is false: wires are used because copper and aluminium are ductile.
o: 2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3
3 only
2 only

questions.q:
(a) Define ductility.
(b) Name two uses of ductile metal wires from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The property by which materials can be drawn into wires. (b) Any two: electrical fittings, ornaments, stringed instruments (veena, sitar, violin, guitar), tea strainer, steel ropes.
s: Part (a): drawn into wires
Part (b): two uses named

questions.q:
A workshop in Pune is fitting a small crane to lift sacks. Its two options are a rope of steel wires and a rope of copper wires of the same thickness. The owner says copper wires are fine because copper wires are used for electrical fittings. The supplier says steel ropes are the ones used in cranes and suspension bridges.
(a) What is steel made of?
(b) Which property lets both metals be made into wires?
(c) Does the chapter give evidence that copper rope can carry heavy loads? Explain.
(d) Which rope should the workshop use? Give your decision and your reason from the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A mixture of iron (a metal) and carbon (a non-metal). (b) Ductility. (c) No. The chapter names copper wires only for electrical fittings; it names steel ropes for cranes and heavy loads. (d) Steel rope, because the chapter says steel wire ropes support heavy loads.
s: Part (a): iron and carbon
Part (b): ductility
Part (c): no evidence for copper ropes
Part (d): steel rope, with reason

questions.q: Why are suspension bridges and cranes fitted with steel ropes rather than ropes made from coal or sulfur? Give reasons from the chapter.
questions.a: Steel is a mixture of iron and carbon that can be drawn into wires, and ropes of steel wires support heavy loads. Coal and sulfur are not ductile, so wires cannot be made of them.
s: Steel wire ropes can support heavy loads
Coal and sulfur are not ductile

questions.q: A visually impaired student taps her stick on a steel gate, a wooden door, a lump of coal and a metal coin placed on the ground. Predict the kind of sound from each, name the property of metals involved, and explain how the sound helps her tell metal from wood.
questions.a: Steel gate and coin: ringing sound; wooden door and coal: dull sound. The property is sonority. The difference between ringing (metal) and dull (wood, coal) lets her tell them apart.
s: Ringing for gate and coin
Dull for door and coal
Names sonority
Links ringing to metals and dull to wood

questions.q: When Ritu drops a steel plate in the school canteen it gives a ringing sound, but a block of wood drops with a dull thud. What does this show?
questions.a: A ringing sound is sonority, a property of metals. Ductility and malleability are different properties and the sound says nothing about softness.
o: The plate is sonorous, which is a property of metals
The plate is more ductile than the wood, so it rings
The wood is more malleable than the plate, so it is dull
The plate is softer than the wood, so it gives a ring

questions.q: One gram of gold can be drawn into a wire 2 km long. (a) How long a wire could be drawn from 5 grams? (b) How much gold would be needed for a 250 m wire?
s: Part (a): 10 km
Part (b): 0.125 g after converting 250 m to 0.25 km

questions.q:
Ananya's music club in Chennai wants a new veena string and a stage bell. For the bell, two plates that look alike are tested by tapping. Plate X gives a ringing sound. Plate Y gives a dull thud, and the shopkeeper admits it is wood painted silver. For the string, the club can pick a drawn metal wire or a thin metal sheet.
(a) Name the property that makes a metal wire possible.
(b) Which plate should the club buy for the bell, and which property did the test show?
(c) Why would a thin metal sheet be wrong for a string even though it is made of metal?
(d) Paint made Y look like metal. Which test is more reliable for the club, looking or tapping? Decide and justify.
questions.a: (a) Ductility. (b) Plate X; it is sonorous. (c) A string must be a wire, drawn through ductility; a sheet is beaten (malleability). (d) Tapping, because sound shows sonority, which painted wood does not have.
s: Part (a): ductility
Part (b): plate X and sonority
Part (c): wire needs ductility, sheet is malleability
Part (d): tapping, with reason

questions.q: A music teacher repairs a violin and replaces its broken string with a thin metal wire. Which property of metals made such a wire possible?
questions.a: A wire is made by drawing the metal, which needs ductility. Malleability gives sheets.
o: Ductility
Malleability
Sonority
Brittleness

questions.q: Aditi puts a metal spoon and a wooden spoon of nearly the same size into a glass of hot water for the same time. When she touches the upper ends the metal spoon is hotter. What does this show?
questions.a: Both spoons were in water of the same temperature for the same time, so the difference is because heat is conducted through the metal and poorly through wood.
o: Heat passes along the metal spoon, so metal is a good conductor of heat
Heat passes along the wooden spoon, so wood is a good conductor of heat
The metal spoon is made heavier, so it holds more heat
The wooden spoon was put into cooler water than the metal spoon

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Cooking vessels are made of metal.
Reason (R): Metals are good conductors of electricity.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but vessels are metal because metals conduct heat. Conducting electricity does not explain it.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I
1. Metal spoon in hot water
2. Rubber gloves
3. Wooden handle of a pan
4. Copper wire in the tester
Column II
a. Protects the electrician from shock
b. Makes the bulb glow
c. Upper end becomes hot
d. Does not pass heat to the hand
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-d, 4-b. The spoon conducts heat, gloves are poor conductors of electricity, the wooden handle is a poor conductor of heat, and copper conducts electricity.

questions.q: Imran joins a cell, a bulb and wires into a tester and connects a piece of coal across the gap. The bulb does not glow. Which conclusion is best supported?
questions.a: A tester bulb glows when the material lets electricity flow easily. It did not, so coal is a poor conductor of electricity.
o: Coal is a poor conductor of electricity
Coal is a good conductor of electricity
Coal is a metal like aluminium and copper
Coal conducts heat but not light

questions.q:
Sunita sets up a tester with a cell, a bulb and wires. She tests five items one at a time: a copper wire, an iron nail, a dry wooden stick, a rubber eraser and a stone. In a separate trial she places a metal spoon and a wooden spoon of nearly equal size in hot water. Her mother wants a pan whose body heats quickly and whose handle stays cool, from copper, iron and wood.
(a) Which items make the bulb glow?
(b) Explain what the spoon trial shows about metal and wood.
(c) Which material should be the handle, and why not the other two?
(d) Which of copper and iron should be the body? Say whether the chapter lets you choose between them.
questions.a: (a) Copper wire and iron nail. (b) Heat travels through the metal spoon, so metals are good conductors of heat; wood is a poor conductor. (c) Wood, because it is a poor conductor of heat, whereas copper and iron conduct heat to the hand. (d) Either; both are metals and good conductors of heat. The chapter does not rank them.
s: Part (a): copper wire and iron nail
Part (b): metal conducts heat, wood poorly
Part (c): wood handle with reason
Part (d): either metal, chapter does not rank

questions.q: Rohit joins a nylon rope into a tester circuit and expects the bulb to glow. Show why it cannot.
questions.a: Nylon rope is a poor conductor of electricity. It does not let electricity flow easily, so the circuit is not completed and the bulb does not glow, as in Activity 4.4.
s: Nylon rope is a poor conductor
Electricity cannot flow through it
Bulb does not glow

questions.q:
(a) What is meant by a good conductor of electricity?
(b) Name two objects from Activity 4.4 that make the bulb glow and two that do not.
questions.a: (a) A material that allows electricity to flow through it easily. (b) Glow: aluminium foil, iron nail, copper wire. Not glow: sulfur, coal, dry wood, stone, rubber eraser, nylon rope (any two each).
s: Part (a): allows electricity to flow easily
Part (b): two glowing and two non-glowing

questions.q: The transfer of heat from one point to another within a material is called
questions.a: Transfer of heat through a material from one point to another is conduction.
o: conduction
corrosion
sonority
malleability

questions.q: Zoya tests an iron key, an aluminium spoon, a plastic scale, a wooden pencil and a stone in a tester circuit. Predict which will make the bulb glow. Then a rod she cannot name also makes the bulb glow. Say what you can and cannot conclude about it from the chapter, and why one result is not enough to decide.
questions.a: Glow: iron key and aluminium spoon. No glow: plastic scale, wooden pencil, stone. The rod that glows is a good conductor of electricity and, since all the materials that glowed were metals, it is likely a metal. The pattern is only a pattern, so more properties (lustre, malleability) should be checked before deciding.
s: Iron key and aluminium spoon glow
Plastic, wood and stone do not glow
The rod is a good conductor
Likely a metal, by the pattern
One property alone is not enough; check others

questions.q: Explain how the conduction of heat makes metal the right choice for a cooking pan and the conduction of electricity makes metal the right choice for an electrical wire. Then give one place where a poor conductor of heat is chosen on purpose and say why, and say which of the two conducting properties a pan does not need.
questions.a: A pan gets heat from the flame and passes it to the food, because metals are good conductors of heat. An electrical wire carries current, because metals are good conductors of electricity. A wooden handle is chosen on purpose because wood is a poor conductor of heat and does not burn the hand. A pan does not need conduction of electricity.
s: Pan: metal conducts heat
Wire: metal conducts electricity
Wooden handle as a poor conductor of heat
Reason for handle: does not pass heat to the hand
Pan does not need electrical conduction

questions.q: Give one everyday situation where a poor conductor of heat is useful and one where a poor conductor of electricity is useful.
questions.a: Wooden handle of a cooking pan keeps the hand safe from heat; the plastic handle of a screwdriver protects the user from electric shock.
s: Poor conductor of heat with its use
Poor conductor of electricity with its use
Explains why in both

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Electricians wear rubber gloves while working.
Reason (R): Rubber is a poor conductor of electricity.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both true. Because rubber does not let electricity flow, the gloves protect from shock: R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Why are cooking vessels made of metal but their handles of wood?
questions.a: Metals are good conductors of heat, so they carry heat to the food; wood is a poor conductor, so the handle does not get hot.
o: Metal passes heat to the food; wood does not pass it to the hand
Metal does not conduct heat, but wood carries it to the food faster
Wood is lustrous and hard, so it can bear the weight of the pan
Wood is ductile, so it can be drawn out into a long handle easily

questions.q: Meena tests only an iron nail in a tester circuit and the bulb glows. She says, 'So every metal is a good conductor of electricity.' Is she right, and is her evidence enough?
questions.a: Partly. The chapter's pattern (aluminium, iron and copper all made the bulb glow) supports that metals are generally good conductors, but one nail alone is not enough to say every metal. Several materials must be tested to see a pattern.
s: Verdict: partly right
Pattern from several metals supports metals as good conductors
One test alone is not enough evidence

questions.q: Why does a screwdriver used by an electrician have a plastic handle while its tip is metal?
questions.a: The metal tip is a good conductor; the plastic covering is a poor conductor of electricity, so it protects the electrician from shock.
s: Plastic is a poor conductor of electricity
Protects from electric shock

questions.q:
(a) Define conduction.
(b) In Activity 4.3 both spoons stay in the same hot water for the same time. Why does that matter for concluding that metals are better conductors than wood?
questions.a: (a) Transfer of heat from one point to another in a material. (b) With the same water temperature and time, the only difference is the material, so the hotter metal spoon shows that metal conducts heat better.
s: Part (a): heat transfer from one point to another
Part (b): only the material differs, so the result is due to the material

questions.q:
A school electrical club must buy 12 screwdrivers. Set A has a plastic handle and costs ₹90 each. Set B has a metal handle covered with a layer of rubber and costs ₹80 each. Both have metal blades. The teacher says the handle is what protects the user, and asks the club to decide.
(a) Why is a covering on the handle needed at all?
(b) Which Activity 4.4 evidence tells you plastic and rubber are safe coverings?
(c) How much does the club save in total by choosing set B over set A?
(d) Which set should the club buy? Decide and give your reason.
questions.a: (a) Metals are good conductors of electricity, so a metal handle would let electricity pass to the user. (b) The chapter says the plastic covering on screwdrivers and rubber gloves protect because these are poor conductors of electricity. (c) 12 x 90 = ₹1,080 for A; 12 x 80 = ₹960 for B; saving ₹120. (d) Set B, since both coverings are poor conductors and B costs less, provided the rubber covering is not damaged.
s: Part (a): metal handle conducts electricity
Part (b): rubber and plastic poor conductors
Part (c): saving ₹120
Part (d): set B with reason

questions.q: Differentiate between a good conductor and a poor conductor of heat, with one example each.
questions.a: A good conductor transfers heat easily (a metal spoon); a poor conductor transfers it poorly (a wooden spoon).
s: Good conductor with example
Poor conductor with example

questions.q: Which statement about conduction is FALSE?
questions.a: False: the wooden spoon stays cooler because wood is a poor conductor of heat. The other statements are in the chapter.
o: A wooden spoon in hot water becomes as hot as a metal spoon at its upper end.
In Activity 4.4, the materials that made the bulb glow were all metals.
The transfer of heat from one point to another in a material is conduction.

questions.q: In the tester circuit of Activity 4.4, which of these makes the bulb glow?
questions.a: Iron is a metal and a good conductor of electricity. Eraser, nylon rope and dry wood are poor conductors.

A rubber eraser
A nylon rope
A piece of dry wood

questions.q:
Read the statements about conduction.
Statement 1: Conduction is the transfer of heat from one point to another of a material.
Statement 2: Wood is a good conductor of heat, which is why cooking vessels have handles of wood.
Statement 3: Metals are generally good conductors of heat and of electricity.

questions.a: 1 and 3 are true. 2 is false: wood is a poor conductor of heat, which is why it is used for handles.
o: 1 and 3 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3
1 only

questions.q: In Activity 4.3 you choose a metal spoon and a wooden spoon 'of almost the same size and thickness'. Why?

Same size makes the test about the material

questions.q: Asha says, 'If I pour away the oil from bottle B and leave the bottle open, the nail in it will rust after a few days.' Do you agree? Explain with the activity.
questions.a: Yes. The oil layer stopped air dissolving into the boiled water. Without it and with the bottle open, air can reach the water, so the nail meets both air and water and rusts.
s: Verdict: agrees
Oil layer was what kept air out
Air and water together make the nail rust

questions.q: A school wants to protect its iron gate, swings and cycle stand from rusting. Explain why it needs to, give two methods from the chapter and say which you would apply to the swings and why.
questions.a: Rusting damages iron structures and an enormous amount of money is spent on repair or replacement every year. Methods: painting, oiling, greasing, galvanisation with zinc. For swings, painting (or galvanisation) gives a protective layer on a surface children handle; oiling or greasing would be messy for hands. Any reasoned choice from the chapter's methods is accepted.
s: Need: costly repair or replacement
First method named
Second method named
Chooses a method for the swings
Gives a sensible reason

questions.q: Which statement about rusting and corrosion is FALSE?
questions.a: False: rust needs both air and water; the nail in bottle B (water alone, no air) did not rust.
o: An iron nail in water alone, with no air at all, will still rust.
A nail kept in dry air alone does not develop any brown deposit.
Galvanisation means applying a protective layer of zinc on iron.
The Iron Pillar of Delhi has barely any rust in spite of its age.

questions.q: State two facts about the Iron Pillar of Delhi from the chapter and say what they tell us about ancient India.
questions.a: It is over 1600 years old (made in the time of Chandragupta II), about 8 m high, over 6000 kg and has barely any rust. It shows the skill developed in metal technology in India.
s: Two facts about the pillar
Skill in metal technology

questions.q:
A school sports store keeps iron hurdles. During the monsoon the hurdles in the open verandah get wet. Plan 1: keep them in a tightly shut store with silica gel packets at ₹150 per month. Plan 2: paint them with a protective coat, twice a year at ₹1,100 each time, and leave them in the verandah. The coach asks for a decision for one year.
(a) Which two conditions make the hurdles rust in the open verandah?
(b) Which condition does silica gel take away in Plan 1?
(c) Work out the cost of each plan for one year.
(d) Which plan would you recommend, and what would you tell the coach about each plan's weakness?
questions.a: (a) Air and water (moist air). (b) Moisture, since silica gel keeps the air dry. (c) Plan 1: 150 x 12 = ₹1,800. Plan 2: 1,100 x 2 = ₹2,200. (d) Plan 1 is cheaper by ₹400 and removes water; its weakness is that the store must stay tightly shut. Plan 2 gives a protective layer but costs more and must be repeated. Plan 1 is the better recommendation on cost; any reasoned choice is accepted.
s: Part (a): air and water
Part (b): silica gel keeps air dry
Part (d): recommends with reasons and weaknesses

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I
1. Silica gel
2. Boiled and cooled water
3. Layer of oil on water
4. Zinc coating on iron
Column II
a. Stops air from dissolving in water
b. Keeps the air dry
c. Removes dissolved gases
d. Galvanisation
Choose the correct pairing.
questions.a: 1-b, 2-c, 3-a, 4-d. Silica gel dries the air, boiling removes dissolved gases, oil blocks air and zinc coating is galvanisation.

questions.q: Two iron buckets stand in a school garden through the monsoon. One is plain; the other is coated with a layer of zinc. After some months only the plain bucket has brown patches. What explains the difference?
questions.a: Galvanisation, a zinc coating, is one of the methods named for preventing rusting. The other options misstate what rust needs or what zinc is.
o: The zinc coating (galvanisation) is a protective layer
Rust needs only water, and zinc keeps the coated bucket dry inside
Zinc is a non-metal, so the coated bucket cannot corrode at all
Zinc changes the iron into silica gel, which absorbs the rain

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rusting of iron is a serious problem in our country.
Reason (R): Only a small amount of money is spent every year to repair or replace rusted iron structures.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: the chapter says an enormous amount of money is spent every year.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Describe a household situation in which an iron object would rust quickly, and then change one thing in it so that rusting is prevented. Name the method.
questions.a: Iron tongs left wet in an open kitchen rust because they meet air and water. Rubbing oil or grease on them, or painting them, prevents rusting.
s: Situation with both air and water
A change that stops rusting
Names the method (painting, oiling, greasing or galvanisation)

questions.q:
(a) Define corrosion.
(b) A copper bowl gets a green coating. Why is this not called rusting?
questions.a: (a) Gradual deterioration of metal surfaces caused by air, water or other substances. (b) Rust is the brown deposit that forms on objects made of iron; the green coating on copper is corrosion of copper.
s: Part (a): gradual damage of metal surfaces by air, water or other substances
Part (b): rust is the brown deposit on iron only; copper's is corrosion

questions.q: The green coating that forms on the surface of a copper object is an example of
questions.a: Gradual damage of metal surfaces by air, water or other substances is corrosion; the green coating on copper is an example.
o: corrosion
galvanisation
sonority
malleability

questions.q: In bottle A of Activity 4.5, what is the purpose of silica gel?
questions.a: Silica gel keeps the air dry. Boiled cooled water removes dissolved gases and the oil layer stops air dissolving.
o: To keep the air in the bottle dry
To supply water to the nail
To remove dissolved gases from water
To stop air from dissolving in the water

questions.q: Ajay says the black coating on his silver ring is rust. Show why this cannot be called rust, and name the process.
questions.a: Rust is the brown deposit on objects made of iron. Silver is not iron, and its black coating is the result of corrosion, the gradual damage of a metal surface by air, water or other substances.
s: Rust is the brown deposit on iron
Silver is not iron
Names the process as corrosion

questions.q: In bottle B of Activity 4.5 the nail is placed in freshly boiled and cooled water and a layer of oil is poured on top. Explain the purpose of each step.
questions.a: Boiling and cooling removes dissolved gases from the water; the oil layer prevents air from dissolving in the water.
s: Boiled water removes dissolved gases
Oil layer stops air dissolving

questions.q: Two new bottles are set up with iron nails. Bottle D has a nail partly dipped in freshly boiled and cooled water with no oil on top, left open. Bottle E has a nail coated thickly with grease, left open in a dish of water. Predict what you expect for D and for E after 10 days, with reasons. Then say what the pair tells you about conditions for rusting.
questions.a: D: the nail will rust, since without the oil layer air can dissolve in the water and reach the nail, so both air and water are present. E: the nail will not rust, since grease is a protective layer that prevents contact with air and water. The pair shows rust needs both air and water together and a protective layer prevents it.
s: D predicted to rust
Reason for D: air reaches the water
E predicted not to rust
Reason for E: protective layer of grease
Conclusion about conditions and prevention

questions.q: Neha sets up three bottles. X: a nail with silica gel, tightly capped. Y: a nail in freshly boiled and cooled water with a layer of oil, tightly capped. Z: a nail partly in water in an open bottle. After 10 days which nails show brown deposits?
questions.a: Rust needs air and water together. X has no moisture, Y has no air; only Z has both.
o: Only the nail in Z
The nails in X and Z
Only the nail in X
The nails in X, Y and Z

questions.q:
Mansi visits the Iron Pillar of Delhi, made in the time of Chandragupta II more than 1600 years ago. It stands about 8 m high, weighs over 6000 kg and has barely any rust. Her grandfather's iron gate has brown patches after a few monsoons, worst where rain collects. A dealer offers painting at ₹2,500 every year, or galvanisation at ₹12,000 once, which he says will last at least 5 years.
(a) What does the pillar's condition say about metal technology in ancient India?
(b) Which two conditions cause the patches, and which one does the rain supply?
(c) Name the zinc-coating process and work out which option costs less over 5 years.
(d) Which option would you advise? Give your decision and reasons.
questions.a: (a) Skills in metal technology were well developed in India. (b) Air and water; rain supplies water. (c) Galvanisation. Painting: 5 x 2,500 = ₹12,500 against ₹12,000 once, so galvanisation costs ₹500 less if the dealer is right. (d) Galvanisation, if the dealer's claim holds, since it is slightly cheaper and gives a protective layer; painting is fine if the family prefers a smaller yearly cost. Any reasoned choice is accepted.
s: Part (a): skill in metal technology
Part (b): air and water, rain gives water
Part (c): galvanisation and the ₹500 difference
Part (d): reasoned recommendation

questions.q:
(a) Define rusting.
(b) Which two things must be present together for it, and which bottle of Activity 4.5 had both?
questions.a: (a) Formation of rust (brown deposit) on objects made of iron. (b) Air and water (moist air); bottle C.
s: Part (a): formation of rust on iron
Part (b): air and water, bottle C

questions.q: Name three methods of preventing rusting. What is meant by galvanisation?
questions.a: Painting, oiling, greasing (or galvanisation). Galvanisation is a protective layer of zinc applied on iron.
s: Three methods named
Galvanisation: zinc coating on iron

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Iron objects left in the open for a few days develop a brown deposit.
Reason (R): Rust forms when iron is in contact with both air and water.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true; moist air in the open supplies both conditions, so R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Read the statements about corrosion and its prevention.
Statement 1: The gradual deterioration of metal surfaces by air, water or other substances is called corrosion.
Statement 2: Painting, oiling, greasing and galvanisation can all be used to prevent rusting.
Statement 3: A copper object kept open in the atmosphere can get a green coating.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: All three statements are in the chapter, so all are correct.
o: 1, 2 and 3
2 and 3 only
1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q: The brown deposit that forms on an iron object left in the open is called
questions.a: The brown deposit on iron is rust; forming it is called rusting.
o: rust
magnesium oxide
sulfurous acid
silica gel

questions.q: Compare magnesium and sulfur on burning in air: the flame or product, what the product does with water and litmus, and the type of oxide. Then say what general rule the chapter draws.
questions.a: Magnesium: dazzling white flame, white magnesium oxide, solution turns red litmus blue, basic. Sulfur: sulfur dioxide gas, forms sulfurous acid in water, turns blue litmus red, acidic. Rule: oxides of metals are generally basic and those of non-metals are acidic.
s: Magnesium flame and product
Magnesium oxide is basic, with litmus test
Sulfur gives sulfur dioxide, acidic, with litmus test
States the general rule for metals and non-metals

questions.q:

(b) Why is the gas jar covered with a lid before water is added and shaken?
questions.a: (a) Burning sulfur produces gases that can be harmful if inhaled. (b) The lid ensures the gas produced does not escape, so it can dissolve in the water added later.
s: Part (a): harmful gases produced
Part (b): lid keeps the gas in so it dissolves in the water

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Burning magnesium ribbon leaves a white powder whose solution turns red litmus blue.
Reason (R): Oxides of metals are generally basic in nature.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both are true; magnesium is a metal, so its oxide is basic, which turns red litmus blue. R explains A.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Read the statements about oxides.
Statement 1: Magnesium ribbon burns with a dazzling white flame, forming white magnesium oxide.
Statement 2: Sulfur dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid.
Statement 3: Oxides of metals are generally basic in nature.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 are true. 2 is false: sulfur does not react with water; it is sulfur dioxide from burning sulfur that forms sulfurous acid in water.

1 only

questions.q: State two properties in which non-metals like sulfur and phosphorus differ from metals and name the nature of their oxides.

s: Two properties
Oxides acidic

questions.a: Sodium is a metal, so its oxide is generally basic and would turn red litmus blue. Phosphorus is a non-metal, so its oxide is acidic and would turn blue litmus red. Rule: oxides of metals are generally basic and those of non-metals are acidic. Sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and water, releasing a lot of heat, and phosphorus catches fire in air, so these are handled by the teacher (demonstration).
s: Sodium oxide predicted basic, red litmus turns blue
Phosphorus oxide predicted acidic, blue litmus turns red
States the rule for metals and non-metals
Sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and water
Phosphorus catches fire in air, so teacher handles both

questions.a: Burning sulfur gives sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid. An acid turns blue litmus red; only a basic solution (like a metal oxide's) turns red litmus blue.
s: Sulfur dioxide forms sulfurous acid
An acid turns blue litmus red
Red-to-blue is for basic metal oxides

(a) Why is sodium stored in kerosene?
(b) Using your answer, explain why sodium cannot be stored in water the way phosphorus is.
questions.a: (a) It reacts vigorously with oxygen and water, releasing a lot of heat; kerosene keeps out air and moisture. (b) Sodium reacts vigorously with water, whereas phosphorus does not and only needs to be kept away from air.
s: Part (a): reacts vigorously with oxygen and water
Part (b): sodium reacts with water, phosphorus does not

A metal such as magnesium
A metal such as sodium
A material such as plastic or rubber

questions.a: Sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and water releasing much heat; kerosene keeps out air and moisture.

catches fire on exposure to air alone, like phosphorus
is a liquid metal at room temperature, like mercury
forms an acidic oxide, like sulfur

questions.q:
A science teacher tests oxides in a demonstration. Element X, a metal, burns with a dazzling white flame and leaves a white powder. Element Y is sulfur, burnt in a deflagrating spoon in a gas jar; the gas is shaken with water. She also shows that Y does not react when placed directly in water. A third element Z is shiny, but its oxide, dissolved in water, turns blue litmus red. A student says, 'Z is a metal because it is shiny.'
(a) State the nature, acidic or basic, of the oxides of X and Y.
(b) Y does not react with water, yet its oxide solution is acidic. Explain.
(c) Which clue about Z points to a non-metal, and which clue the student used points to a metal?
(d) Should the student's statement be accepted? Decide, and say what further test you would do.
questions.a: (a) X's oxide is basic; Y's oxide is acidic. (b) Burning Y makes sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in water to form sulfurous acid; Y itself does not react with water. (c) The acidic oxide points to a non-metal; shininess (lustre) points to a metal. (d) No. The clues conflict, and a single property is not enough. Test hammering (malleability) or conduction before deciding; the chapter says oxides of non-metals are acidic.
s: Part (a): basic for X, acidic for Y
Part (b): the oxide, not sulfur itself, forms the acid
Part (c): acidic oxide: non-metal; shine: metal
Part (d): does not accept; proposes a further test

questions.q:

questions.a: (a) A substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances. (b) Metals and non-metals are elements; plastic, glass, wood, rubber and paper are materials, not elements.
s: Part (a): cannot be broken down into simpler substances
Part (b): metals and non-metals are elements, plastic and wood are not

questions.q: In a demonstration, sulfur burns in a deflagrating spoon inside a covered gas jar. Water is then added and the jar is shaken. Strips of blue and red litmus paper are dipped into the liquid. What will the teacher see?
questions.a: Burning sulfur gives sulfur dioxide, which forms sulfurous acid in water; the solution is acidic and turns blue litmus red (as in the chapter's Fig. 4.7d).

Red litmus turns blue; blue litmus stays blue
Neither paper changes, since sulfur does not react with water
Both papers turn blue

questions.q: Phosphorus is stored in water because it
questions.a: Phosphorus catches fire in atmospheric air, so it is kept under water, with which it does not react.
o: catches fire when exposed to air
reacts vigorously with water, like sodium
is a liquid at room temperature, like mercury
is dull and brittle, like coal

questions.q: Which of these is NOT classified as a metal or a non-metal because it is not an element?
questions.a: Plastic, glass, wood, rubber and paper are materials, not elements. Carbon, phosphorus and nitrogen are non-metal elements.
o: Plastic
Carbon
Phosphorus
Nitrogen

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.

1. Magnesium ribbon burning

b. Solution turns blue litmus red

questions.a: 1-c, 2-a, 3-b, 4-d. Magnesium gives a white powder, sodium is kept in kerosene, burnt sulfur gives an acidic solution and phosphorus is kept in water.

questions.q: Rohit says plastic is a non-metal because it is not a metal. Check his claim with the chapter.
questions.a: No. Metals and non-metals are elements. Plastic, glass, wood, rubber and paper are materials that are not elements, so they are neither.

Plastic and similar materials are not elements

questions.q:

questions.a: A is false: sulfur does not react with water. R is true; it is sulfur dioxide, the oxide formed on burning, that gives the acidic solution.

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: A solution of magnesium oxide in warm water changes the colour of
questions.a: Magnesium oxide solution turns red litmus blue, so it is basic. Blue turning red would mean acidic.

blue litmus paper to red

questions.a: False: sulfur does not react with water. The other statements are in the chapter.

questions.q:

questions.a: (a) Kerosene, because sodium reacts vigorously with oxygen and water and kerosene keeps out air and moisture. questions.q:

questions.a: (a) White magnesium oxide, from the reaction of magnesium with oxygen in the air. (b) Dissolve in warm water; the solution turns red litmus blue.

Part (b): turns red litmus paper blue

questions.q: Write a short lab note describing how you would find whether the oxide of an element is acidic or basic.
questions.a: Burn the element, collect the oxide, dissolve it in water, test with blue and red litmus; red turning blue means basic, blue turning red means acidic.
s: Burn and collect the oxide
Dissolve in water and test with litmus
Interprets colour change

questions.q:
A village health camp has a budget of ₹5,000. A well's water has to be made safe to drink, a boy has a scraped knee, and a farmer wants to know what to add to the soil of his wheat field to improve plant growth. The camp can buy chlorine for ₹1,800, iodine solution for ₹900 and a nitrogen fertiliser for ₹2,600.

questions.a: (a) Chlorine. (b) Iodine solution, an antiseptic. (c) Nitrogen, an essential nutrient for plant growth. (d) Total ₹1,800 + ₹900 + ₹2,600 = ₹5,300, which is ₹300 over. The fertiliser serves the farmer, not the camp's health work, so drop it (any reasoned choice is accepted).
s: Part (a): chlorine
Part (b): iodine antiseptic
Part (c): nitrogen, a plant nutrient
Part (d): ₹5,300 total and a reasoned item to drop

questions.q:

questions.a: A is false: the chapter stresses that non-metals matter (oxygen, carbon, nitrogen, chlorine, iodine). R is true.

Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q: How do the properties of metals and non-metals decide their uses in everyday life? Give two uses of metals linked to their properties, one use of a non-metal and one alloy, and say what a good choice of material means.

An alloy use
Concludes property matched to the job

questions.q: What is an alloy?

questions.q:

questions.q: A farmer's wheat grows poorly. An extension officer suggests a fertiliser. Which non-metal element is an essential nutrient for plants and is used to make fertilisers?

Chlorine
Iodine
Oxygen

questions.q:

questions.q:

Statement 1: Zirconium is used in aerospace and titanium in atomic energy.
Statement 2: Steel is a mixture of two non-metals, iron and carbon.
Statement 3: Alloys are mixtures of two or more metals or of a metal and a non-metal.

questions.a: Only 3 is correct. 1 is false: zirconium is used in atomic energy and titanium in aerospace. 2 is false: iron is a metal, carbon a non-metal.

1 and 2 only

questions.q: An eco club collects old aluminium and iron scrap from the neighbourhood and sends it for recycling. What is the main benefit the chapter points to?
questions.a: Many metals, especially iron and aluminium, are recycled in India to minimise waste and contribute to sustainability.

It makes the metals rust-proof
It makes the metals more ductile than before
It lets the metals be stored in kerosene

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Iron and aluminium are recycled in India.
Reason (R): Zirconium is used in atomic energy.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both statements are true, but the use of zirconium has nothing to do with why iron and aluminium are recycled.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Which statement about non-metals, alloys and recycling is FALSE?
questions.a: False: steel is a mixture of iron (a metal) and carbon (a non-metal). The other statements are in the chapter.
o: Steel is a pure metal with nothing else mixed into it.
Nitrogen is an essential nutrient for the growth of plants.
Titanium is a metal that is used in the aerospace industry.
Iron and aluminium are metals that are recycled in India.

questions.q: A village school can afford only one of three items this month: chlorine for its water tank, iodine solution for its first-aid box, or a nitrogen fertiliser for its kitchen garden. Name what each does, choose one to buy first and justify it, and say what you lose by not buying the others.
questions.a: Chlorine purifies water; iodine solution is an antiseptic for wounds; nitrogen in fertilisers is an essential nutrient for plants. Any one can be chosen with a reason, e.g. chlorine because safe water affects every student daily. Not buying iodine leaves wounds without an antiseptic; not buying fertiliser reduces garden growth.
s: Chlorine use
Iodine solution use
Nitrogen fertiliser use
A choice with a reason
Consequence of not buying the others

questions.q: Why is carbon called the building block of all life forms? Name the three kinds of substances in which it is a key component.
questions.a: Carbon is a key component of proteins, fats and carbohydrates, which are necessary for growth and energy in all life forms.
s: Carbon in proteins, fats and carbohydrates
Needed for growth and energy

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Steel is an alloy.
Reason (R): Steel is a mixture of two metals only.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true. R is false: steel is a mixture of a metal (iron) and a non-metal (carbon).
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: Which non-metal do we breathe in to survive?
questions.a: We breathe in oxygen, a non-metal. Zirconium, titanium and aluminium are metals.
o: Oxygen
Zirconium
Titanium
Aluminium

questions.q:
A school eco club runs a scrap drive in Jaipur. The collected items are aluminium foil trays, iron rods, steel spoons and plastic bottles. The club has space for only two kinds of items for recycling this month and wants to follow the chapter.
(a) Which two metals does the chapter say are recycled in India?
(b) What is one benefit of recycling them?
(c) Are steel spoons made of a single metal? Explain.
(d) The club must choose two kinds of items from the four. Decide which, and say why the chapter does not support choosing the plastic bottles.
questions.a: (a) Iron and aluminium. (b) It minimises waste and contributes to sustainability. (c) No. Steel is an alloy of iron (a metal) and carbon (a non-metal). (d) Aluminium foil trays and iron rods (steel spoons also contain iron). The chapter names only iron and aluminium for recycling and does not mention plastic.
s: Part (a): iron and aluminium
Part (b): waste reduction, sustainability
Part (c): steel is an alloy
Part (d): chooses metal items; plastic not in the chapter

questions.q: A shopkeeper labels a steel almirah as 'pure iron, an element'. Show why this cannot be correct, using the chapter's meaning of alloy and element.
questions.a: Steel is a mixture of iron and carbon, so it is an alloy, not a pure metal. An element is a substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances; steel contains two different elements mixed together.
s: Steel is a mixture of iron and carbon
An element cannot be broken into simpler substances
Steel contains two elements, so it is not an element

questions.q: Describe a neighbourhood situation in which recycling iron or aluminium helps, and state the benefit the chapter mentions.
questions.a: A colony collects used aluminium or iron objects and sends them for recycling; this minimises waste and contributes to sustainability.
s: A realistic recycling situation
Names iron or aluminium
States waste reduction and sustainability

questions.q: Which non-metal is commonly used in water purification?
questions.a: Chlorine is used to purify water. Iodine solution is an antiseptic; nitrogen is used for fertilisers; carbon is the building block of life.
o: Chlorine
Iodine
Nitrogen
Carbon

questions.q: Dev says, 'Steel is an alloy, so it must be a mixture of metals only.' Check his claim with the chapter.
questions.a: No. The chapter says an alloy is a mixture of two or more metals or of a metal and a non-metal. Steel is a mixture of iron (a metal) and carbon (a non-metal).
s: Verdict: wrong
Alloy can be metal plus non-metal
Steel is iron plus carbon
